title: Medicine and the Four Humors
objective: After this level you can explain medieval ideas about health and healing.
summary: Medieval medicine sought balance among four humours. Physicians read urine and let blood to remove an excess; bloodletting was later discredited.

cards.headline: A medieval physician might hold your urine up to the light and study it.
cards.body: He was hunting for clues about four liquids that, he believed, ran your whole body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Welcome to the four humours.

cards.headline: Four liquids in balance
cards.body: The theory was ancient. Hippocrates championed it, and Galen, Rome’s leading medical authority in the 2nd century CE, built on it; it was still current throughout the Middle Ages. The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler) and black bile (melancholy). The ideal person had them perfectly balanced, and illness meant one had got out of proportion. Health was a recipe, and sickness meant too much of one ingredient.

cards.headline: Reading the signs
cards.body: So how do you spot an imbalance you can’t see? Medieval physicians examined a patient’s urine: its colour, its consistency, its clarity and any sediment, all read as signs of the humours inside. A flask held up to the window was the medieval version of a lab test.

cards.headline: Letting out the excess
cards.body: If one humour was in excess, healers tried to remove it, by letting blood or applying leeches. After a church edict of 1163 barred clergy from bloodletting, barber-surgeons took it up alongside shaving and pulling teeth, a legacy you can still see in the barber’s pole. Bloodletting lost credibility in the 18th and 19th centuries, when studies showed it worked less well than claimed.
cards.callout: This is the history of an idea, not medical advice

cards.headline: Words that outlived the theory
cards.body: A person ruled by one humour was called sanguine (from the Latin for blood), phlegmatic, choleric or melancholic. The theory is long discredited, but the words stayed in English. To a medieval doctor, a sanguine friend was simply someone with plenty of blood.

mascot.line: Next time someone seems melancholic, remember: a medieval doctor would have blamed black bile.

cards.headline: The four humours: understood
learned: Four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile
Health meant balance; illness meant excess
Physicians read urine; healers let blood

questions.prompt: Which four humours did medieval medicine believe governed the body?

options.label: Earth, air, fire and water
options.rationale: Those are the four classical elements.

options.label: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile

questions.explanation: The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler) and black bile (melancholy).

questions.prompt: Why did medieval healers let blood from sick people?

options.label: To remove an excess humour and restore balance
To test the blood for germs
Because the Church required it every month
options.rationale: The Church barred clergy from doing it.

questions.explanation: Humoral theory said illness came from imbalance, so healers removed the “excess” humour by bloodletting or leeches.

questions.prompt: How does a modern barber’s pole connect to medieval medicine?

options.label: Medieval monks cut hair in hospitals
options.rationale: Clergy were barred from bloodletting in 1163.

options.label: Physicians hung poles to show urine colours
